grh_d3e16bb033fc75fee067.title: The Lady Takes a Chance
paragraphs: New York bank teller Molly J. Truesdale spends her savings on a fourteen-day guided tour of the West, expecting scenery and a brief escape from her orderly life. At a rodeo she literally catches cowboy Duke Hudkins when a bronco throws him, and the chance meeting turns into a romance. Molly abandons part of her scheduled tour to travel with Duke and his friend Waco, discovering that life with a cowboy means rough roads, horses, camp food, and a man who is far more comfortable making decisions than discussing feelings. Their attraction repeatedly collides with Mollyâ€™s independence and Dukeâ€™s stubbornness, and she finally returns to New York convinced the adventure is over. Duke follows her there, sweeps her back onto the same western bus route, and announces that they will marry when the bus reaches Phoenix. Molly protests every step of the way, but this time she willingly takes the chance on him.

This [[show|screen-directors-playhouse|Screen Directors Playhouse]] broadcast aired on June 28, 1951. It is listed as episode 109 in the archive. [[org|org.f2f0561f0ce2ddc5|NBC Radio Network]] carried the broadcast. The cast includes Joan Caulfield, [[person|john-lund|John Lund]], GeGe Pearson, Jim Backus, and Whitfield Connor. Other credited names include Bill Cairn as director, Howard Wiley as producer, William Hanson as radio adaptor, William Seiter as host, and Jimmy Wallington as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 60 minutes. The broadcast is also associated with [[org|org.0ee8343bca2245d4|Chesterfield]] and [[org|org.50075df24f7e1a61|Anacin]].
This version presents a radio version of [[work|work.sdp.film.74e8b492bde6b2be|The Lady Takes a Chance]]. William Hanson adapted it for radio.

grh_d3afcfaebf6c10145097.title: Cajun Death
paragraphs: Anthropologist Deborah Simms comes to the Louisiana bayou town of Mercy to research local folklore and the stories surrounding her late grandmother, Marie 'Mamrie' Simms, whom residents feared as a loup-garou witch. Townspeople soon suspect Deborah has inherited the same powers and blame her for bad crops, empty fishing nets and other misfortunes. After a pregnant woman gives birth to a stillborn child shortly after Deborah visits the family, an angry mob pursues her into the swamp. Deborah escapes by boat with her tape recorder while the hunters follow. In the darkness they encounter strange lights, frightening animal sounds and the unmistakable voice of Mamrie warning them never to harm her family again. The mob flees and Deborah returns safely. Her recorder has malfunctioned, however, and when asked whether the supernatural voice somehow came from her, Deborah can only say she honestly does not know.

[[org|org.8480b75bc0c36e4b|CBS Radio Network]] carried the broadcast. The cast includes Barney Phillips, Don Diamond, Eddie Firestone, Len Birman, and Lillian Buyeff. Other credited names include Elliott Lewis as director, Elliott Lewis as producer, William Froug as writer, and [[person|vincent-price|Vincent Price]] as host.
The broadcast is also associated with [[org|org.9b0a0ccffce2f7d3|Sears, Roebuck and Company]].

grh_d3e4c8d3a8c997af7bb2.title: The Decoration
paragraphs: A young Soviet woman has been rewarded with a red-star decoration for proving her loyalty by informing on her own father for listening to forbidden broadcasts. Later she travels abroad on a covert mission with her small daughter Ella, carrying concealed instructions while trying to appear harmless. At an American checkpoint, Ella sees a Christmas-tree star and innocently says she wants a decoration like her mother's. In exchange for the promise of one, the child explains how her mother earned the first medal and reveals that the supposedly innocent doll and wrapping conceal a secret, repeating against her mother the same kind of betrayal her mother once committed against her grandfather.

The cast includes Marsha Kimmet, Kate Wilkinson, Evie Juster, Abby Lewis, and Owen Jordan. Other credited names include Ted Bell as director, Joseph Cochran as writer, and Fred Foy as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 20 minutes.
